analysis.one_liner: Restricts attorney fee awards for people and groups that win lawsuits against federal agencies.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late June 2026 with 2 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would sharply limit when someone who wins a lawsuit or case against a federal agency can have their attorney fees paid by the government. Only plaintiffs with a direct monetary stake — a personal injury, property damage, or unpaid benefits — would qualify, awards would be capped at $200,000 per case, and settlements with agencies could no longer include fee payments. It would also require a review of the bill's effects on federally managed forests and rangelands.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that face lawsuits from environmental and public interest groups over federal land, logging, mining, and permitting decisions — such as timber and forest products companies — benefit because the groups suing them would mostly lose the ability to recover attorney fees. The federal government also saves money by paying fewer fee awards. Social Security and veterans benefits attorneys are explicitly carved out of the caps, preserving their fee stream.

how_it_helps.text: Bars fee awards to any party that lacks a 'direct and personal monetary interest' in the case, such as a personal injury, property damage, or unpaid agency payment — which excludes the nonprofit and public interest organizations that typically sue federal agencies over regulations and land management.

Caps fee awards at $200,000 per case and 3 cases per calendar year, unless the case is a class action or involves the Social Security Administration or Department of Veterans Affairs — capping the financial exposure that agencies and the industries they regulate face from fee-shifting suits.

Prohibits any settlement agreement or consent decree that produces a regulation or guidance document from including payment of attorneys' fees or litigation costs, cutting off the 'sue and settle' route where an agency resolves a lawsuit by agreeing to a rule and paying the plaintiff's fees.
Carves out Social Security and Veterans Affairs cases from the caps entirely, preserving the existing fee arrangements for attorneys representing disability and benefits claimants.

Requires the Interior Secretary to convene a review panel on the bill's effects on federally managed lands, with guaranteed seats for the forest products industry and a rural water utility alongside hunters, anglers, and a wildlife biologist.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary citizens and the nonprofits that represent them. Public interest, environmental, civil rights, and watchdog groups would bear litigation costs they can no longer recover from the government even when they win, which would shrink their capacity to challenge agency decisions in court. Individuals with diffuse, non-monetary harms — for example, neighbors of a polluting facility — would also lose fee recovery. The Treasury saves money, but that saving comes from fewer checks on agency power.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public interest groups and ordinary citizens

drawbacks.text: Fee-shifting under the Equal Access to Justice Act is what makes it financially possible for small nonprofits and ordinary people to challenge the federal government, since losing such a case normally means eating years of legal costs; cutting off recovery for anyone without a direct monetary stake would leave agencies' regulatory and land management decisions largely unchallenged.

People harmed in ways that don't show up as a direct dollar figure — such as communities affected by pollution or by weakened safety rules — could win their case and still walk away owing their own legal bills.

The blanket ban on fees in consent decrees removes a tool agencies use to resolve litigation; settling disputes without paying fees may push more cases into full trials and appeals, which costs the government and taxpayers more, not less.

The requirement that courts 'shall' reduce fee awards commensurate with any pro bono hours a lawyer worked could discourage attorneys from volunteering free legal help, since donated hours would directly shrink their paid compensation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would save the federal government and regulated industries money on fee awards, and its sponsors frame it as stopping agencies and advocacy groups from trading friendly settlements for fee payments. The cost falls on the public side of the ledger: the fee-recovery system it dismantles is what lets private citizens and small organizations afford to hold federal agencies accountable in court, and this bill removes that mechanism for most of them. An honest supporter would have to concede that the savings come largely from making public enforcement cases financially impossible.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on June 30, 2026, and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any other action while the session runs out.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Tiffany introduced the bill on June 30, 2026, joined by Rep. Harriet Hageman as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, its only action in the record.
The full action history shows no committee hearing, no markup, no vote, and no further movement after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed yet. Public interest and environmental groups keep the current fee rules, and the timber, mining, and energy interests the bill would shield from fee-shifting lawsuits have not gotten that protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Harriet Hageman
for.what_they_did: Joined as a cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 30, 2026, and has taken no action on the bill since.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the only people attached to the bill are a Republican sponsor and 2 Republican cosponsors, with no Democratic support on record.

industries.note: The bill's fee restrictions would make it much harder for environmental groups to recover legal costs when they challenge federal logging and land management projects, reducing the litigation risk around timber sales on public land. The bill even reserves a seat for a forest products industry affiliate on the review panel that would assess its effects.

industries.industry: Environmental and public interest law organizations
industries.note: Groups that sue federal agencies over regulations, pollution, and land decisions generally lack a direct personal monetary interest, so they would be barred from fee recovery and their cases capped or feeless in settlements. These groups are the public's main private check on federal agency decisions, and this bill defunds that work.

industries.industry: Mining, oil, and gas on federal land
industries.note: Companies and permittees operating on federally managed lands face frequent lawsuits from conservation groups; capping and restricting fee awards raises those groups' cost of suing, giving operators more room to proceed with fewer legal challenges.

industries.industry: Social Security and veterans benefits attorneys
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts cases involving the Social Security Administration and Department of Veterans Affairs from its caps, preserving the existing fee arrangement for lawyers representing disability and benefits claimants. Claimants with unpaid agency disbursements would also keep qualifying under the new monetary-interest test.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one sponsor, 2 cosponsors, and no committee action more than a year before the session ends on January 3, 2027. Bills referred to the Judiciary Committee at this stage with this level of support almost never reach the floor; the most likely outcome is that it dies in committee when this Congress ends.
